title: Where Did Noah's Ark Land? 4 Answers
notes: Beat 2 of QUILL's draft ('no verified Ark') moved to beat 14 so the hook is not killed; it is still said plainly once. Everything else as written.

beats.text: Four mountains claim they hold Noah's Ark.
Case one: Mount Ararat, Turkey, rising five thousand one hundred metres.
It's the famous pick, near the borders with Armenia and Iran.
Case two: near Doğubayazıt, a boat-shaped mound shows up in 1959 aerial photos.
Ron Wyatt promoted it, yet most geologists call it natural.
beats.scene: boat-shaped mound on a hillside, a question mark
beats.source: claim by Ron Wyatt; geology consensus

beats.text: But Genesis 8:4 says 'the mountains of Ararat'. Plural. Not one peak.
beats.scene: the word MOUNTAINS splits into many peaks

beats.text: Ararat is Urartu, an ancient kingdom ruled from Tushpa, near modern Van.
So 'Ararat' may mean a whole highland region.
Case three: Mount Judi near Şırnak, favored by old Syriac Christian tradition.
The Quran, Hud 11:44, says the ship settled on al-Judi.
beats.scene: 'al-Judi' glows, then fades to the map

beats.text: Case four: Pir Omar Gudrun in Iraqi Kurdistan, linked by some to Babylonian flood tablets.
In Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim's boat lands on Mount Nimush, and that match is only proposed.
beats.scene: clay tablet, a small boat on a peak

beats.text: He sends out a dove, a swallow, then a raven.
beats.scene: three birds leave the boat one after another

beats.text: Plainly: no verified Ark has ever been found.
Four peaks, four traditions, one very old question.
Ararat, Durupınar, Judi or Gudrun: which gets your vote?

Four mountains, four traditions, and one verse that says "mountains" plural. Which case file convinces you?
No verified Ark has ever been found. These are claims, shown as claims.
